title: Two fans click the same seat. Who gets it?

scenes.heading: Two fans click the *same seat*
scenes.narration: Two fans click the same concert seat at the same moment. Your code checks that it's free, then sells it. So who gets the seat?

scenes.title: Check, then write
scenes.narration: Checking, then writing, is two steps, so both fans see it's free, and both write: two tickets, one seat. The fix is one statement: mark that seat sold, only where it's still free.

scenes.title: One winner
scenes.narration: The database runs it as one step. The first request changes one row and wins. The second changes zero rows, so that fan picks another seat. That's the price of never selling twice.

scenes.title: One winner
scenes.narration: Check and write in one step: one fan wins, the other picks again. Have you ever been double-booked? The full video is on the channel.

notes: The atomic step is a conditional update, then check the affected row count. In PostgreSQL (Read Committed) the second UPDATE waits for the first, re-checks its WHERE on the new row version and changes zero rows. Alternatives: a row lock (SELECT … FOR UPDATE) or a version column (optimistic locking).
The price: the fan who loses the race has to pick another seat. For groups, sell all the seats in one transaction, all or nothing; the rows stay locked a little longer, so other buyers wait.
The full video covers what comes next: holding the seat while the fan pays, payment failures, and the traffic of a huge sale.

titles: Two Fans Click the Same Seat. Who Gets It?
publish.description: Two fans click the same concert seat at the same moment. How a one-step conditional update makes sure only one of them gets it, and what that costs.
extra: 🎬 The full video (from 500 seats to millions of fans: atomic updates, seat holds, payments and a waiting room) is on the channel.
